author: Han Kang
introFa: کتاب «Human Acts» نوشته Han Kang یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Human Acts»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: In this study, we investigated the regulatory role of RA in IgA CSR in human tonsillar B cells. RA alone induced IgA production exclusively. Furthermore, at the clonal level, limiting dilution analysis was used to demonstrate the role of RA as an IgA isotype switch factor. Further, we found that the RARa mediated RA- induced IgA expression. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Abs and other reagents All protocols were approved by the ethics committee of Kangwon National University. Anti-IgM (DA4.4, IgG1) and anti- CD40 (G28.5, IgG1) Abs were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA). Recombinant IL-4 was prepared in our laboratory [20]. Anti-human IgA-unlabeled 2.2. B cell preparation and cell culture Human tonsillar B cells were prepared as described previously [21]. Mononuclear cells were subjected to two rounds of T cell depletion by rosetting with SRBCs. This resulted in CD20+ B cells comprising more than 95% of the residual population, as assessed by FACSCalibur (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA). A total of 2  105 - cells/well were cultured in ﬂat-bottomed, 96-well tissue culture plates (SPL, Seoul, Korea) in 200 ll of complete medium containing anti-IgM (1 lg/ml), anti-CD40 Ab (1 lg/ml), and IL-4 (50 U/ml). When necessary, RA (Sigma–Aldrich, St. Louis, MO), TGF-b1 (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN), LE540 (Wako Pure Chemical Industries Ltd, Osaka, Japan), and AM80 (Tocris Bioscience, Bristol, UK) were added to cultures. 2.3. Isotype-speciﬁc ELISA and ELISPOT assay ELISAs were performed as described previously [22]. The reac- tion products were measured at an absorbance of 405 nm with an ELISA reader (VERSAMAX reader, Molecular Devices, Sunnyvale, CA). Isotype-speciﬁc ELISPOT assays were performed as described previously [23]. Data are presented as the number of spot-forming cells per 2  105 cultured cells. 2.4. Limiting dilution analysis For limiting dilution analysis, B cells were cultured at various cell densities in round- bottomed, 96-well plates in a ﬁnal volume of 200 ll of complete medium. A total of 96 replicate cultures were set up at each cell density. Cultured wells were individually assayed for the number of IgA-secreting cells by ELISPOT assay after 6 days of culture. Cultures with spot-forming cells were scored as positive. Calculations to determine the frequency of B cells secreting IgA were based on Poisson distribution analysis [24]. The frequency of negative responses at each input number of B cells was used to construct a plot of the log10 of the percentage of negative cultures verses the total number of cultured B cells. Poisson distribution laws predict a straight line that extrapolates to 100% negative responses in cultures with no IgA-secreting B cells. The frequency of IgA-secreting B cells was derived graphically, as demonstrated in the ﬁgure, by interpolating the cell number at which 37% of cul- tures were negative. This yields a cell number at which, on average, there is one IgA-secreting clone per culture. The average size of IgA-secreting clones was calculated using the input number of B cells at which 37% of the cultures were neg- ative. At this input number, the positive cultures contained an average of one precursor per culture. Statistical analysis Statistical differences between experimental groups were determined by analyzing variance, and values of p < 0.05 according to the unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test were considered statis- tically signiﬁcant. 3. Results and discussion 3.1. Effect of RA on Ig secretion by human tonsillar B cells We have recently shown that RA functions as an IgA switch fac- tor in murine B cells and is more speciﬁc than TGF-b1 [17]. TGF-b1 directs IgA isotype switching in both murine and human B cells [5,6]. However, whether RA also exhibits this activity in human B cells remains unknown. Therein, we ﬁrst measured Ig secretion by tonsillar B cells in response to RA or TGF-b1. RA increased IgA secretion by 2–3-fold, but not IgG and IgM (Fig. 1A). Here, TGF- b1, unlike RA, did not increase IgA secretion. There are no signiﬁcant changes in Ig production under the inﬂuence of RA and TGF-b1 in combination. In our previous study with mouse B cells, we observed that IgA secretion was further enhanced when RA is removed from the media after 2 days of culture [17]. We tested this possibility by changing media as shown in Fig. 1B. How- ever, the increase in IgA secretion induced by RA was similar to that observed in the absence of a media change. In the media-chan- ged condition, a low concentration of TGF-b1 (0.05 ng/ml) increased IgA secretion unlike the media-unchanged condition (Fig. 1B). These observations warrant comment. It has been shown that induction of IgA production by membrane IgA negative (mIgA) B cells require neutralization of TGF-b1 activity by anti- TGFb1 Ab for 24 h after the initial setup of the cultures [6]. Our results are consistent with this data in principal since IgA produc- tion increased after TGF-b1 was removed from the media after 2 days of culture (Fig. 1B). In this regard, it appears that RA is more favorable than TGF-b1 in the context of IgA induction. We have demonstrated that the anti-proliferative activity of both TGF-b1 and RA on mouse B cells can contribute to IgA expression on their own [17,23]. Therefore, we hypothesized that the discrepancy in IgA induction patterns between the two mediators is attributed to their different anti-proliferative potencies. We determined the effects of RA and TGF-b1 on human B cell growth and proliferation using trypan blue exclusion and CFSE analysis, respectively (Fig. 2). RA and TGF-b1 inhibited tonsillar B cell growth, with the latter showing greater suppression than the former. Taken together, these results suggest that RA acts as speciﬁc IgA inducer, and that, once IgA isotype switching is over, RA little affects IgA B cell differ- entiation while TGF-b1 down-regulates. RA-induced IgA produc- tion was not diminished by anti-pan TGF-b Ab, and RA did not enhance TGF-b1 expression in tonsillar B cells (data not shown), indicating that the RA-mediated IgA secretion is not associated with TGF- b1 activity. Since RA speciﬁcally stimulates tonsillar B cells to produce IgA, we were interested in determining which subclass was affected. enhanced the secretion of both IgA1 and IgA2, although the optimal RA concentrations for induction differed: 25 nM for IgA1 and 5 nM for IgA2 (Fig. 3). In contrast, the various concentrations of RA examined did not affect IgG and IgM production. These results reveal that RA speciﬁcally increases IgA production without a preference in IgA subclass. 3.2. RA increases IgA isotype switching at the clonal level Because RA directly modulates B cells to differentiate into IgA B cells, it was necessary to investigate whether RA increased the total number of IgA-secreting cells or simply the amount of IgA secreted per cell. As shown in Fig. 4A, there was an increase in the number of IgA1-secreting cells in RA-stimulated cultures. We subsequently performed a limiting dilution analysis to distinguish whether increases in the number of IgA1-secreting cells in the above exper- iments was: (1) due to an increase in the frequency of B cells that switch to the IgA isotype after RA stimulation, or (2) due to increased proliferation of B cells that are already committed to express the IgA isotype. Activated human tonsillar B cells were cul- tured in limiting dilution with RA as described previously [23]. As shown in Fig. 4B, RA stimulated a 2.4-fold increase in the frequency of IgA1-secreting B cell clones among populations of activated ton- sillar B cells without increasing the number of IgA1-secreting B cells per clone. These data indicate that RA is a bona ﬁde IgA switch factor. TGF-b1 also increases GLTa1/GLTa2 expression and subsequent IgA1/IgA2 secretion in human B cells [9]. Therefore, expression of GLTa1 and GLTa2 can be used to indicate active IgA CSR. Because RA increased IgA isotype switching at the clonal level, it was nec- essary to determine whether RA has such an effect at the molecular level. Indeed, RA increased the expression of GLTa1 and GLTa2 while decreasing the expression of other GLTs such as GLTc1 and GLTe (Fig. 4C). In this, RA enhanced the expression of AID. These results indicate that RA increases IgA CSR by inducing both GLTa and AID expression. The RA-enhanced expression of AID has been previously demonstrated in mouse B cells [26], while RA little affect AID expression in our study [17]. These discrepancies are likely due to different cell stimulating conditions and remain to be determined. 3.3. RA speciﬁcally increases IgA CSR through RAR It is well known that RA activates target genes mainly through RAR [27]. In human tonsillar B cells, RARa is expressed at a higher level compared to RARb and RARc [18]. Therein, we tested the effect of AM80, a RARa agonist, on IgA production. As shown in Fig. 5A, AM80 increased IgA1 secretion to the level induced by RA but not IgG and IgM. Furthermore, LE540, a RAR antagonist, abrogated the increase in IgA1 and GLTa1 induced by RA (Fig. 5B). These results suggest that RA induces IgA1 CSR mainly through RARa. In conclusion, we demonstrate that RA selectively induces IgA isotype switching in human B cells. It has been shown that RA accelerates the differentiation of human B cells into mature plasma cells [18]. RA is synthesized from precursor molecules such as ret- inol in GALT-DCs [28]. GALT-DC-derived RA induces the expression of the gut-homing receptors a4b7 integrin and CCR9 in mouse and human B cells [13]. In addition, RA induces homing of protective T and B cells to the gut after subcutaneous immunization in mice [29]. Together, it is highly plausible that RA plays an important role in the intestinal IgA Ab response in humans. Finally, since RA also induces gut-homing Foxp3+ regulatory T cells from naive human T cells [30], it is possible that RA plays pivotal roles in maintaining overall mucosal homeostasis in humans.
